en: Theravāda Vinayapiṭaka Cūḷavagga 16.
Senāsanakkhandhaka (The Chapter on Lodgings)
1. The Allowance for Monasteries.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, lodgings had not yet been assigned by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus.
And those bhikkhus dwell here and there—
in the forest, at the foot of a tree, on a mountain, in a cleft, in a mountain cave, in a charnel ground, in a jungle thicket, in the open air,
or on a heap of straw. At the proper time, they emerge from their respective places.
In forest retreats, at the foot of trees, on mountains, in gorges, mountain caves, cemeteries, jungle thickets, in open spaces, or on heaps of straw—
graceful in their advancing and retreating, in their looking ahead and looking aside, in their drawing in and extending of limbs, with downcast eyes,
they were perfected in the postures of deportment.
Now at that time, the merchant of Rājagaha went to the park early in the morning.
There he saw those bhikkhus emerging from here and there early in the morning—
from the forest, from the foot of trees, from mountains, from ravines, from mountain caves, from cemeteries, from remote jungle-thickets, from open spaces, and from heaps of straw.
He was pleasing in his advancing and retreating, in his looking ahead and looking aside, in his bending and stretching;
with downcast eyes, he was perfected in his deportment.
Having seen him, his mind became serene.
Then the merchant of Rājagaha approached those bhikkhus and, having approached them, said to them:
"Venerable sirs, if I were to have monasteries built, would you dwell in my monasteries?
"Householder, monasteries have not yet been authorized by the Blessed One."
“In that case, venerable sir, please ask the Blessed One about this and let me know.
“Very well, householder,” those monks replied to the merchant of Rājagaha. They then approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side.
As they were sitting to one side, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, the merchant of Rājagaha wishes to have a monastery built.
How, venerable sir, should we proceed?”
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma on this occasion and in this context, addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, bhikkhus, five kinds of shelters:
a vihāra, an aḍḍhayoga, a pāsāda, a hammiya, and a guhā.”
Then those bhikkhus approached the merchant of Rājagaha, and having approached him, they said this to the merchant of Rājagaha:
“Householder, the Blessed One has authorized the construction of monasteries;
now do as you think it is time to do.”
Then the merchant of Rājagaha established sixty monasteries in a single day.
Having completed those sixty monasteries, the merchant of Rājagaha approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the merchant of Rājagaha said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept my meal for tomorrow, together with the community of bhikkhus.
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then the merchant of Rājagaha, understanding the Blessed One’s consent, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
Then, at the end of that night, the merchant of Rājagaha had various kinds of fine food, both hard and soft, prepared and had the time announced to the Blessed One:
"It is time, venerable sir; the meal is ready.

Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to the residence of the merchant of Rājagaha. Having arrived, he sat down on the seat prepared for him together with the community of monks.
Then the merchant of Rājagaha, having personally served and satisfied the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha with excellent hard and soft foods,
sat down to one side when the Blessed One had finished his meal and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl.
As he was sitting there, the merchant of Rājagaha said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, these sixty dwellings were built by me seeking merit and seeking heaven.
Venerable sir, how should I proceed regarding these dwellings?
“In that case, householder, establish those sixty dwellings for the Saṅgha of the four quarters, both present and future.”

“Yes, venerable sir,” the merchant of Rājagaha replied to the Blessed One, and he established those sixty dwellings for the Saṅgha of the four quarters, both those who had arrived and those yet to come.
Then the Blessed One expressed his appreciation to the merchant of Rājagaha with these verses:
“They ward off cold and heat...”
Then there were wild beasts,
and snakes, mosquitoes,
and also cold and rains.
Then, when a fierce wind and heat arise, it is warded off;
for the sake of shelter and for the sake of comfort,
For one who meditates and practices insight,
the gift of a dwelling to the Saṅgha is praised as the foremost by the Buddha.
Therefore, indeed, a wise person,
clearly perceiving his own welfare,
should have delightful monasteries built.
One should cause those who are learned to dwell here, providing them with food,
drink, clothing, and lodging.
One should give to those who have become upright with a serene mind;
they will teach the Dhamma to him.
The dispelling of all suffering:
having understood this Dhamma here,
he attains final Nibbāna, free from taints.
Then the Blessed One, having expressed his appreciation to the merchant of Rājagaha with these verses, rose from his seat and departed.
Hearing that "the Blessed One has indeed authorized monasteries," people had monasteries constructed with great care.
Those dwellings were without doors;
even snakes, scorpions, and centipedes entered them.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a door-panel,” [the Blessed One said].
Having made a hole in the wall, they fastened the door-panel with creepers or ropes;
yet it was still eaten by rats and termites.
The door-panels fell because their fastenings had decayed.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a wooden frame, a mortar-shaped bolt, and an upper crossbar.”
The door panels would not close.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a hole for pulling and a cord for pulling,” he said.
The doors would not stay shut.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a door-bolt, a door-latch, a pin, and a bolt-hook.”
Now at that time, the bhikkhus were unable to open the door.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, bhikkhus, a hole for a key.”
There are three kinds of locks:
the iron lock, the wooden lock, and the horn lock.
When these are opened and they enter, the dwellings remain unguarded.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a wooden needle-case,” he said.
Now at that time, the dwellings were thatched with grass.
"In the cold season it was cold, and in the hot season it was hot.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
"Monks, I allow you to plaster [the walls] inside and out after first smearing them with mud."
Now at that time, the dwellings were without windows, causing eye-strain and being foul-smelling.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
"Monks, I allow three types of windows: [the window with bars, the window with lattices, and the window with shutters]."
“There are the railing windows, the lattice windows, and the slat windows.
Monkeys and bats were entering through the gaps between the windows.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow, monks, a window-screen,” [the Blessed One said].
Even with a window-screen, bats and flying foxes would enter.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow, monks, a window shutter and a window screen.
Now at that time, the monks were sleeping on the ground;
their limbs and their robes became covered in dust.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a grass mat,” he said.
However, the grass mat was eaten by rats and termites.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, a massage,” he said.
But from the massage, their limbs became painful.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a bedstead made of split bamboo,” he said. 2.
The Allowance of Bedsteads, Stools, and Other Furnishings.
Now at that time, a couch made of masāraka wood had been offered to the Saṅgha.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, a couch made of masāraka wood,” he said.
A seat made of *masāraka* wood appeared.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, a seat made of *masāraka* wood,” he said.
Now at that time, a bed with a headboard made of bound wood was offered to the Saṅgha.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, a bed with a headboard made of bound wood,” he said.
A bench with a backrest appeared.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a bench with a backrest,” he said.
Now at that time, a bed with crab-shaped legs had been acquired for the Saṅgha.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, a bed with crab-shaped legs,” he said.
A stool with crab-shaped legs appeared.
They informed the Blessed One of this matter.
“Monks, I allow a stool with crab-shaped legs,” he said.
Now at that time, a bed with detachable legs had been obtained for the Saṅgha from a charnel ground.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, a bed with detachable legs,” he said.
A bench with detachable legs arose.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a bench with detachable legs,” he said.
Now at that time, a high-backed chair had been obtained for the Saṅgha.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, a high-backed chair,” he said.
A high chair was offered to them.
They informed the Blessed One of this matter.
“Monks, I allow even a high chair,” he said.
The seven-limb [meditation] arose.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow the seven-limb,” he said.
A high seven-piece [robe] came into existence.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow even a high seven-piece [robe],” he said.
A bhaddapīṭha chair arose [as a need].
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, a bhaddapīṭha chair,” he said.
A bench arose [as a need].
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
"I allow you, monks, a bench," he said.
A stool with goat’s-foot legs arose.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, I allow a stool with goat’s-foot legs.”
A stool with rounded legs made of *āmalaka* wood appeared.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a stool with rounded legs made of *āmalaka* wood.”
A wooden board appeared.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a wooden board,” he said.
A backrest arose.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, I allow a backrest.”
A straw mat arose.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, I allow a straw mat.”
Now at that time, the group of six monks were lying on high beds.
People, while wandering on a tour of the monasteries, saw them and complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying,
"They are just like householders who indulge in sensual pleasures."
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, one should not lie on a high bed.
Whoever should so lie down commits an offense of wrong-doing.”
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu, while lying on a low bed, was bitten by a snake.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow, bhikkhus, bed-leg supports,” [the Blessed One said].
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks were using high bedstead legs; with those bedstead legs, they shook [the beds].
People, while wandering on a tour of the monastery, saw this and complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying, "They are just like householders who indulge in sensual pleasures."
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, high bed-legs must not be used.
Whoever should use them, there is an offense of wrong-doing.”
“I allow, monks, bedstead supports no more than eight finger-breadths [in height].
Now at that time, thread had come to the Saṅgha.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, to wrap a bed with thread.
The limbs consumed too much thread.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, having pierced the limb, to wrap it with a cross-shaped bandage.
A cloth was required;
they reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, to make a mattress-cover,” he said.
A stuffed mattress (tūlikā) arose;
they reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, having disentangled it, to make a pillow.
There are three kinds of stuffing:
tree-down, vine-down, and grass-down.”
Now at that time, the group of six monks were using bolster pillows for their bodies.
People, while wandering on a tour of the monasteries, saw them and complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying,
"They are just like householders who indulge in sensual pleasures."
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, half-body pillows should not be used.
Whoever should use one, there is an offense of wrong-doing.”
“I allow you, monks, to make a pillow the size of the head.
Now at that time, there was a festival on the mountain peak in Rājagaha.
People were preparing cushions for the high officials.
There were woolen mattresses, cotton mattresses, bark-fiber mattresses, grass mattresses, and leaf-mattresses.
When these had been discarded at the festival site, they dragged them away after tearing off the outer skin.
The monks saw much wool, cotton, bark-fiber, grass, and leaves strewn about at the place of the festival.
Having seen this, they reported the matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, I allow five kinds of mattresses:
a wool mattress, a cotton mattress, a bark-fiber mattress, a grass mattress, and a leaf mattress.”
Now at that time, cloth for bedding belonging to the Saṅgha had been acquired.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, to cover a mattress with it,” he said.
Now at that time, the monks were spreading a mattress for a bed-frame upon a chair, and a mattress for a chair upon a bed-frame.
The mattresses were torn apart.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, a covered bed and a covered chair.
They spread it out without making a canopy, and it fell down from below... [etc.
... “I allow you, monks, having made a canopy and having spread it out, to cover it with a mattress.”
They tore off the skin and carried it away...
[as before] ... "I allow you, monks, to sprinkle it," he said.
Yet they still carried it away... [as before] ...
“I allow you, monks, the work of plastering.
They nevertheless continued to carry it away...
[as before] ... “I allow you, monks, the work of hand-plastering.”
“They indeed carry it away…” [etc.
… “I allow, monks, hand-food. 3.
The Allowance for White Color, etc.
Now at that time, the beds of the sectarians were white in color, the ground was blackened, and the walls were treated with red ocher.
Many people went there seeking beds.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow, monks, white color, black color, and the application of red ocher in the dwelling.
Now at that time, the white color would not adhere to a rough wall.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, having given a lump of husks and having rubbed with the hand, to apply white color.
White color was difficult to fix...
“I allow you, monks, having applied fine clay and having rubbed with the hand, to apply white color.”
A white color was difficult to fix...
[omission] ... "Monks, I allow you to use *ikkāsa* plaster.
Now at that time, the red ochre did not adhere to a rough wall.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to apply red ocher after giving a ball of husks and striking with the hand.
The red ocher was not adhering... [as before]...
“I allow you, monks, after applying a paste of fine clay and smoothing it with the hand, to apply red ocher.
The red ocher would not adhere...
[as before] ... “I allow you, monks, crushed mustard seeds and beeswax mixed with oil.”
"It becomes too thick...
[as before] ... 'Monks, I allow you to remove it with a cloth.
Now at that time, on rough ground, the black dye did not settle.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you, having given a lump of husks and having warded it off with the hand, to apply a black color.
The black color was difficult to fix... [as before]...
“I allow you, monks, having applied a medicinal clay poultice and having rubbed with the hand, to apply a black dye.
The black dye was difficult to fix...
[as before] ... “I allow you, monks, a decoction of *ikkāsa* as a fixative.”
4. Prohibition on Painted Decorations.
Now at that time, the group of six monks had painted decorations made in their dwellings—images of women and images of men.
People, while wandering on a tour of the monasteries, saw this and complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying,
"They are just like householders who indulge in sensual pleasures.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, a decorative design should not be made— neither the form of a woman nor the form of a man.
Whoever should have one made commits an offense of wrong-doing.”
“I allow, monks, floral designs, creeper designs, shark-tooth patterns, and the fivefold pattern.
Now at that time, the dwellings had low foundations and were being submerged by water.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, to build it on a high foundation,” he said.
But the structure collapsed... [as before]...
“I allow you, monks, to build three kinds of structures:
a structure of bricks, a structure of stone, and a structure of wood.
While they were ascending, they suffered distress... [and so on].
“I allow you, monks, three kinds of stairs:
brick stairs, stone stairs, and wooden stairs.
As they were ascending, they fell... [and so on].
“I allow, monks, a leaning board.
Now at that time, the dwellings were made of *āḷakamanda* (reeds).
The monks felt ashamed to lie down.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, a window-screen,” he said.
They lifted up the window-screen and looked out... [and so on].
“I allow you, monks, a half-wall.
The half-walls looked down from above...
[as before] ... “I allow you, monks, three types of enclosures:”
"A palanquin chamber, a pillar chamber, a balcony chamber.
Now at that time, the monks were constructing chambers in the middle of small dwellings;
there was no surrounding space.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to construct a small inner chamber in a small dwelling, and one in the center of a large one.
Now at that time, the corner pillar of a dwelling was decaying.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a wall-socket,” he said.
The wall of the dwelling leaked... [and so on].
“I allow, monks, a protective screen with a fringe.
Now at that time, a snake fell onto the shoulder of a certain monk whose hut was thatched with grass.
Terrified, he let out a cry.
The bhikkhus ran up to that bhikkhu and said to him,
“Friend, why did you cry out?
Then he informed the bhikkhus of the matter.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a canopy,” he said.
Now at that time, the monks were hanging bags from the legs of the beds and the legs of the benches.
"They were being eaten even by ants and termites.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
"Monks, I allow a wall-peg and a wall-bracket."
Now at that time, the monks were leaving their robes on couches and chairs,
and the robes became torn.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow, monks, a clothes-pole and a clothes-line in the dwelling.
Now at that time, the dwellings were without porches and lacked shelter.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow, monks, a porch, a vestibule, a gallery, and a portico.
The porches became exposed.
The monks felt ashamed to lie down there... [and so on].
“I allow, monks, a sliding door and a hinged door.
Now at that time, monks who were taking their meal in the open air were distressed by both the cold and the heat.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, a meeting hall,” he said.
The meeting hall had a low foundation and was flooded with water... [as before] ...
“I allow you, monks, to build on a high foundation.
The structure collapsed... [etc. ...
“I allow you, monks, to build three types of structures: a stone structure, a brick structure, and a wooden structure.”
"A brick staircase, a stone staircase, and a wooden staircase.
Ascending them, they were distressed...
[as before] ... "Monks, I allow three kinds of staircases: [brick, stone, and wood]."
“There are brick stairs, stone stairs, and wooden stairs.
As they were climbing up, they fell down...
[and so on] ... “Monks, I allow a handrail.”
Grass and dust were falling into the assembly hall...

[as before] ... "I allow you, monks, having smeared it with mud, to plaster it inside and out—to apply white color, black color, red ocher, floral designs, creeper designs, shark-tooth patterns, fivefold borders, a robe-pole, and a robe-rope."
Now at that time, the monks were spreading out their robes on the bare ground in the open air.
The robes became covered in dust.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow, monks, a clothes-pole and a clothes-line in the open air.
The drinking water became contaminated...
[as before] ... “I allow, monks, a water-hall and a water-shed.”
The water-hall had a low foundation and was flooded by water...
[as before] ... "Monks, I allow you to build it on a high foundation.
The masonry collapsed... [as before] ...
“I allow you, monks, to build three kinds of structures:
a brick structure, a stone structure, and a wooden structure.
While ascending, they were distressed... [and so on].
“I allow you, monks, three kinds of stairs:
brick stairs, stone stairs, and wooden stairs.
While ascending, they fell down... [and so on].
“I allow you, monks, a support-beam.
Grass and dust fell from the water-hall... [as before] ...
“I allow you, monks, having smeared it with mud, to plaster it inside and outside.”
“White-colored, black-colored, prepared with red ocher, floral designs, creeper designs, shark-tooth patterns, five-fold borders, robe-poles, and robe-strings.
A water vessel was not available... [as before] ...
“Monks, I allow a water-conch and a water-scoop.”
7. The Allowance for Enclosures, etc.
At that time, the monasteries were unenclosed.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, to enclose [the monastery] with three kinds of walls:
a wall of brick, a wall of stone, and a wall of wood.
There was no gatehouse... [and so on].
“I allow, monks, a gatehouse,” he said.
The gatehouse had a low foundation and was flooded by water...
[as before] ... “I allow, monks, to build it on a high foundation,” he said.
The storehouse had no door. [As before...
"Monks, I allow a door, a wooden frame, a bolt, an upper bolt, a bolt-pin, a door-latch, a keyhole, a pin, a knob, a hole for the bolt, a hole for the pull-cord, and a cord for pulling.
Straw and dust fell into the storehouse. [As before...]
“I allow you, monks, having leveled the ground, to plaster it inside and out—
white color, black color, an application of red ochre, floral designs, creeper designs, shark-tooth patterns, and the fivefold checkerboard.
Now at that time, the courtyard was muddy.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to scatter gravel,” he said.
They were still not able to master it. … [as before] …
“I allow you, monks, to set down a stone slab.
Water collected there...
[as before] ... “I allow you, monks, a water drain.”
Now at that time, the monks were making fireplaces here and there in the courtyard.
The courtyard became filthy.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to build a fire-hall on one side.
The fire-hall had a low base and was flooded by water...
[as before] ... “Monks, I allow you to build it with a high base.”
A cairn collapsed... [as before] ...
"Monks, I allow you to build three types of cairns:
a brick cairn, a stone cairn, and a wooden cairn."
“Those who were climbing up were becoming exhausted.
… [as before] … “Monks, I allow three kinds of stairs:
brick stairs, stone stairs, and wooden stairs.”
"As they were climbing up, they fell down...
[as before] "...I allow you, monks, a handrail.
There was no door for the fire hall... [as before] ...
“I allow, monks, a door, a wooden frame, a mortar, an upper bolt, a door-socket, a knob, a pin, a bolt, a keyhole, a hole for drawing [water], and a rope for drawing.
Grass and dust fell into the fire-hall...
[as before] ... “I allow, monks, having plastered it inside and out, to make it smooth.”
“White color, black color, preparation with red ochre, floral designs, creeper designs, shark-tooth patterns, five-fold borders, robe-poles, and robe-strings.
At that time, however, the monastery was unfenced.
Jackals and dogs were also harassing them on the upper terraces.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to enclose it with three walls.”
"The bamboo fence, the thorn-fence, and the trench.
There was no enclosure wall.
Just as before, the goats and sheep harassed the crops in the fields. …pe…
“I allow, monks, a gatehouse, a threshold, double doors, an archway, and a crossbar.
Grass and dust fell into the gatehouse...
[as before] ... “I allow, monks, having plastered it inside and out, to make it smooth.”
“White color, black color, preparation with red ochre, floral designs, creeper designs, shark-tooth patterns, and the fivefold pattern.
The monastery grounds were muddy...
[as before] ... “I allow you, monks, to scatter sand.”
They could not master it...
[as before] ... "Monks, I allow you to lay down a stone slab.
The water stood still... [as before] ...
“I allow, monks, a water drain.
Now at that time, King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha desired to have a palace built for the Saṅgha, plastered with lime and clay.
Then it occurred to the monks:
“What, indeed, has been permitted by the Blessed One as roofing material, and what has not been permitted?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow five kinds of roofing materials:”
“Roofing with bricks, roofing with stone, roofing with plaster, roofing with grass, and roofing with leaves.
The first recitation section is finished.
1. The Story of Anāthapiṇḍika.
Now at that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was the brother-in-law of the guild-president of Rājagaha.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika went to Rājagaha on some business.
At that time, the guild-president of Rājagaha had invited the Saṅgha, headed by the Buddha, for the following day's meal.
Then the merchant of Rājagaha gave orders to his slaves and laborers:
“In that case, my men, rise early and cook the rice gruels, cook the meals, prepare the soups, and prepare the side dishes.
Then it occurred to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika:
“Formerly, householder, when I arrived, this man would set aside all his duties and exchange greetings with me alone.
But now, appearing distracted, he is ordering his slaves and laborers:
‘Well then, men, having risen early, cook the rice gruels, cook the meals, prepare the soups, and prepare the side dishes.’”

"Could it be that this householder has a son coming for marriage, or a daughter going for marriage, or perhaps a great sacrifice is being prepared, or has King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha been invited for tomorrow’s meal along with his army?
Then the merchant of Rājagaha, having given orders to his slaves and laborers, approached the householder Anāthapiṇḍika;
having approached him and exchanged greetings with the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, he sat down to one side.
As the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was sitting to one side, he said this to the merchant of Rājagaha:
“Formerly, householder, when I arrived, you would set aside all your affairs and exchange greetings with me alone.
But now, you appear distracted as you issue orders to your slaves and laborers.”
"In that case, my man, rise early and cook the rice porridges, cook the meals, prepare the soups, and prepare the side dishes.

What is it, householder? Is there to be a wedding, or a marriage, or has a great sacrifice been prepared, or has King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha been invited for tomorrow’s meal along with his army?"
“Householder, there will be no wedding for me, nor will there be a marriage; nor has King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha been invited with his army for tomorrow’s meal.
Rather, a great sacrifice is prepared for me;
the Saṅgha, headed by the Buddha, has been invited for tomorrow.”
“‘Buddha,’ householder, do you say?
“‘Buddha,’ householder, I say. “‘Buddha,’ householder, do you say?”
“I say, householder, ‘a Buddha. “Do you say, householder, ‘a Buddha’? “I say, householder, ‘a Buddha.’”
“Householder, this too is rare in the world, namely, ‘a Buddha,
a Buddha. Is it possible, householder, at this time to approach that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One, for the sake of seeing him?”
“Householder, it is not the right time to approach the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, at this moment.
You shall approach that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, for a visit at a later, more appropriate time.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika—
"Thinking, 'In time, I shall go to see that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One,' Anāthapiṇḍika the householder lay down with mindfulness directed toward the Buddha;
indeed, three times during the night he rose, thinking it was dawn.
Then Anāthapiṇḍika the householder approached Sīvaka Gate."
The non-human beings opened the gate.
Then, as the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was departing from the city, the light vanished, darkness appeared, and fear, trepidation, and horripilation arose within him;
he then desired to turn back right there.
Then the yakkha Sivaka, having vanished, made this sound heard:
"A hundred elephants, a hundred horses,
and a hundred chariots drawn by mules."
A hundred thousand maidens,
adorned with jeweled earrings,
[are not equal] to a single stride forward.
They are not worth a sixteenth part of it.
Come forward, householder! Come forward, householder!
It is better for you to come forward than to retreat.”
Then the darkness vanished for the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, and light appeared.
Whatever fear, trepidation, and horripilation he had experienced subsided.
A second time also... [and so on].
A third time, the light for the householder Anāthapiṇḍika vanished, darkness appeared, and fear, trepidation, and horripilation arose; he then desired to turn back from that very spot.
A third time, the yakkha Sivaka, having become invisible, let out a shout:
“A hundred elephants, a hundred horses,
a hundred chariots with mules,
and a hundred thousand maidens— ”
Though adorned with jeweled earrings,
they are not worth even a sixteenth part of a single stride of one who has set out on the path.
"Come forward, householder! Come forward, householder!
It is better for you to come forward than to turn back.
For a third time, the darkness vanished for the householder Anāthapiṇḍika and light appeared; whatever fear, trepidation, and horripilation he had experienced subsided.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the Cool Grove.
Now at that time, the Blessed One, having risen during the last watch of the night, was walking back and forth in the open air.
The Blessed One saw the householder Anāthapiṇḍika coming from afar.
Having seen him, he descended from the walkway and sat down on the prepared seat.
Once seated, the Blessed One said this to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika:
"Come, Sudatta."
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika,
thinking, "The Blessed One addresses me by name," was joyful and elated;
he approached the Blessed One, and having approached, he prostrated with his head at the Blessed One’s feet and said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I hope the Blessed One slept well?
“The brahmin who has attained final nibbāna always sleeps in peace.”
He who is not smeared by sensual desires,
become cool and free from acquisitions,
having cut through all attachments—
Having removed the dart from his heart,
being at peace and having attained tranquility with his mind, he sleeps happily.
Then the Blessed One gave the householder Anāthapiṇḍika a graduated discourse, namely:
a talk on giving, a talk on virtue, and a talk on heaven; he revealed the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit in renunciation.

When the Blessed One knew that the householder Anāthapiṇḍika had a ready mind, a pliant mind, a mind free from hindrances, an uplifted mind, and a confident mind, he then set forth that teaching on the Dhamma which is uniquely realized by Buddhas.
Suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

Just as a clean cloth, free from dark stains, would properly take up the dye, even so, while sitting right there, the dustless, stainless eye of Dhamma arose in the householder Anāthapiṇḍika: [that whatever is subject to origination is subject to cessation].
“Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, having seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, and plunged into the Dhamma;
having crossed over doubt and being free from perplexity, having gained intrepidity and becoming independent of others in the Teacher’s instruction, said this to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Bhante! Magnificent, Bhante!

Just as, Bhante, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms; [so has this been made clear by the Blessed One.]”
In this very way, the Blessed One has proclaimed the Dhamma by means of many methods.
Venerable sir, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.
“Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept my meal for tomorrow, together with the community of bhikkhus.
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, understanding the Blessed One’s consent, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
The merchant of Rājagaha heard:
"It seems the householder Anāthapiṇḍika has invited the Saṅgha, headed by the Buddha, for tomorrow’s meal.
Then the merchant of Rājagaha said this to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika:
“It seems, householder, that she has invited the Saṅgha, headed by the Buddha, for tomorrow’s meal.
And you are a newcomer.
Householder, let me give you the means whereby you may provide a meal for the Saṅgha, headed by the Buddha.”
“Enough, householder; I have the means by which I shall provide a meal for the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.
Now the merchant guild of Rājagaha heard:
“It seems the householder Anāthapiṇḍika has invited the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha for tomorrow’s meal.”
Then the merchant guild of Rājagaha said this to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika:
“Householder, it seems you have invited the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha for tomorrow’s meal.
And yet, you are a newcomer.”
“Householder, give me some goods so that you may provide a meal for the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.
“Enough, venerable sir;
I have goods with which I shall provide a meal for the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.”
King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha heard:
“It seems that the householder Anāthapiṇḍika has invited the Saṅgha, headed by the Buddha, for tomorrow’s meal.
Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha said this to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika:
“Householder, it seems the Saṅgha, headed by the Buddha, has been invited by her for tomorrow’s meal.
And you are a newcomer.
Householder, let me give you some capital with which you may provide a meal for the Saṅgha, headed by the Buddha.”
“Enough, Your Majesty;
I have the means by which I shall provide a meal for the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.
Then, when that night had passed, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika had exquisite hard and soft foods prepared in the residence of the Rājagaha merchant and had the Blessed One informed that it was time.
“Venerable sir, it is time; the meal is ready.

Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to the residence of the merchant of Rājagaha. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat together with the community of monks.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika [served] the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, with excellent hard foods...

Having personally served and satisfied him with various kinds of food, and when the Blessed One had finished his meal and withdrawn his hand from the bowl, Anāthapiṇḍika the householder sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, he said to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept from me a residence for the rains at Sāvatthī together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus."
“Householder, the Tathāgatas indeed delight in empty dwellings.
“Understood, Blessed One; understood, Sugata,” he replied.
Then the Blessed One, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the householder Anāthapiṇḍika with a discourse on the Dhamma, rose from his seat and departed.
Now at that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was one who had many friends, many companions, and whose word was respected.
Then, having settled his business in Rājagaha, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika set out for Sāvatthī.
Along the way, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika gave orders to the people:
“Noble ladies, establish monasteries, build dwellings, and set up offerings.
A Buddha has appeared in the world, and that Blessed One has been invited by me; he will come along this path.”
Then those people, dismissed by the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, prepared the monastery grounds, established the dwellings, and set up offerings.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, having gone to Sāvatthī, looked all around Sāvatthī, thinking:
"Where might the Blessed One dwell?"
"It should be neither too far from the village nor too close, suitable for coming and going,
accessible to people whenever they need it, with little crowding by day, quiet and free from noise at night,
secluded from people, private, and appropriate for seclusion."
The householder Anāthapiṇḍika saw Prince Jeta’s park—
it was neither too far from the village nor too near, well-situated for coming and going, accessible to people whenever they wished,
with little bustle by day, and quiet, still, and free from noise at night, secluded from people, and suitable for retreat.
Seeing that it was suitable for seclusion,
he approached Prince Jeta and, having approached him, said this to Prince Jeta:
"Give me your park, noble son, so that I may make it a monastery."
“Householder, this monastery cannot be accepted even for the price of ten million pieces of gold.
“The monastery is accepted, noble sir,” [the householder said].
“The monastery is not accepted, householder,” [the son replied].
They asked the chief ministers of justice, “Was it taken or was it not taken?
The ministers replied,
“Since you, noble son, set the price, the monastery has been taken.”
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika had gold carried out on carts and had the Jeta Grove covered with a layer of crores.
When the gold that had been carried out once was not sufficient for even a small area around the gatehouse,
the householder Anāthapiṇḍika gave orders to his men:
“Go, my good man, bring gold;
we shall spread it over this area.
Then it occurred to Prince Jeta:
“This cannot be a trifling matter, since this householder is giving away so much gold.
He said to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika:
“Enough, householder! Enough!”
"Do not have that place spread out for him.
Give this place to me; this gift shall be mine."
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika thought:
"This Prince Jeta is well-known and of recognized standing;
moreover, it is of great significance for such a person of recognized standing to have faith in this Dhamma and Vinaya."
He gave that site to Prince Jeta.
Then Prince Jeta had a gateway built on that site.
Subsequently, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika had monasteries constructed in Jeta’s Grove, he had courtyards constructed, and he had gateways constructed.
He had [monasteries] built; he had assembly halls built; he had fire-halls built; he had kitchens built; he had latrines built;
he had walking-paths built; he had walking-path halls built; he had wells built; he had well-halls built;
he had bath-houses built; he had bath-house halls built; he had lotus ponds built.
He had [them] built; he had pavilions built.
2. The Gift of Building Projects.
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Rājagaha for as long as he pleased, set out on a wandering tour toward Vesālī.
Wandering by stages on his alms tour, he arrived at Vesālī.
There, the Blessed One stayed at Vesālī in the Gabled Hall in the Great Wood.
Now at that time, people were engaged in building new works with great care.
Those monks who undertake new building projects also attend to them with care, providing robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
Then, a certain poor tailor thought:
"This cannot be a trivial matter, since these people are performing the new building work so diligently."
“What if I were to do some construction work myself?
Then that poor tailor, having personally kneaded mud and piled up bricks, raised a wall.
Because he was unskilled, the crooked wall he had built collapsed.
A second time...
and a third time, that poor weaver, having himself trampled the mud and piled up bricks, erected a wall.
Because of his lack of skill, the crooked wall collapsed.
Then that poor tailor complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
"Those who give these recluses, sons of the Sakyans, robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, they exhort and instruct them, and they assign new building-work to them.
But as for me, I am poor."
"No one is advising me, nor instructing me, nor assigning me new work.
The monks heard that poor weaver complaining, grumbling, and carping.
Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma on this occasion and in this connection, addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, bhikkhus, to assign building work.
A bhikkhu assigned to building work, bhikkhus, will exert himself.”
‘How indeed might this dwelling come quickly to its completion?
He will repair what is broken and dilapidated.
And furthermore, monks, it should be given in this way:
First, a monk should be requested; having been requested, a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha may assign the new construction work on the dwelling of the householder named so-and-so to the monk named so-and-so.”
This is the motion.
Let the Sangha, venerable sirs, hear me:
the Sangha grants the supervision of the new construction of the dwelling of the householder named so-and-so to the bhikkhu named so-and-so.
Whichever venerable one approves of the gift of this householder’s dwelling for the new construction work of this monk, let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
The Saṅgha has granted the householder [named] so-and-so’s dwelling for the new construction work of the monk [named] so-and-so.
“The Saṅgha consents, therefore it is silent; thus do I hold this.
3. The Granting of the Best Seat, etc.
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Vesālī for as long as he pleased, set out on a wandering tour toward Sāvatthī.
Now at that time, the monks who were pupils of the group-of-six monks went ahead of the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha and took possession of the dwellings, taking possession of the beds, thinking:
"This shall be for our preceptors; this shall be for our teachers; this shall be for us."

Then the Venerable Sāriputta, following closely behind the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, found no place to rest when the dwellings had already been assigned and the beds had already been allotted; he sat down at the foot of a certain tree.
Then, as the night was passing into dawn, the Blessed One stood up and coughed.
The Venerable Sāriputta also coughed.
“Who is here?
“It is I, Blessed One, Sāriputta.
“Why are you sitting here, Sāriputta?”
Then the Venerable Sāriputta reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, on this occasion and in this connection, having had the community of monks assembled, questioned the monks:
"Is it true, monks, that the resident pupils of the group-of-six monks go ahead of the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha and take possession of monasteries and take possession of beds?"
“Will this be for our preceptors? Will this be for our teachers? Will this be for us?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them... [as before]...

"How indeed, monks, could those foolish men go ahead of the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha and take possession of the dwellings, taking possession of the beds—thinking, 'This shall be for our preceptors,' 'This shall be for our teachers,' or 'This shall be for us'?
This, monks, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence... [and so forth]."
Having rebuked them … and having given a teaching on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus,
who is worthy of the best seat, the best water, and the best almsfood?”
Some monks said this:
"Lord, one who has gone forth from a khattiya family deserves the best seat, the best water, and the best almsfood.
Some other monks said this:
“Blessed One, one who has gone forth from a brahmin family deserves the best seat, the best water, and the best alms-food.
Some monks said this:
“Blessed One, one who has gone forth from a householder’s family deserves the best seat, the best water, and the best alms-food.”
Some bhikkhus said this:
“Venerable sir, one who is a master of the discourses deserves the foremost seat, the foremost water, and the foremost almsfood.
Some other bhikkhus said this:
“Blessed One, he who is a master of the Vinaya deserves the foremost seat, the foremost water, and the foremost alms-food.
Some other monks said, “Blessed One,
he who is an expounder of the Dhamma deserves the foremost seat, the foremost water, and the foremost alms-food.”
Some bhikkhus said this:
“Venerable sir, one who has attained the first jhāna deserves the best seat, the best water, and the best almsfood.
Some other bhikkhus said this:
“Blessed One, one who has attained the second jhāna deserves the best seat, the best water, and the best almsfood.
Some other bhikkhus said:
“Blessed One, one who has attained the third jhāna deserves the best seat, the best water, and the best almsfood.”
Some bhikkhus said this:
"Venerable sir, one who has attained the fourth jhāna deserves the best seat, the best water, and the best almsfood.
Some other bhikkhus said this:
“Blessed One, one who is a stream-enterer is worthy of the best seat, the best water, and the best almsfood.
Some other bhikkhus said:
“Blessed One, one who is a once-returner …” [and so on].
“Whoever, Blessed One, is a non-returner … whoever,
Blessed One, is an arahant, he is worthy of the foremost seat, the foremost water, and the foremost almsfood.
Some other bhikkhus spoke thus:
“Blessed One, one who possesses the threefold knowledge deserves the foremost seat, the foremost water, and the foremost almsfood.
Some other bhikkhus said:
“Blessed One, one who possesses the six direct knowledges deserves the foremost seat, the foremost water, and the foremost almsfood.”
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
"Once upon a time, bhikkhus, there was a great banyan tree in the Himalayan region.
Three friends lived depending upon it."
The partridge, the monkey, and the elephant.
They lived together without mutual respect, without deference, and without harmonious conduct.
Then, monks, it occurred to those companions:
‘Oh, surely we would know who among us is greater by birth; we would honor him, revere him, respect him, and worship him, and we would abide by his instruction.
Then, monks, the partridge and the monkey asked the elephant:
‘Friend, what do you remember from the past?’
“When I was a young calf, friend, I would pass between the thighs of this banyan tree, and its topmost sprout would touch my belly.
This, friend, I remember from the past.
Then, monks, the partridge and the elephant asked the monkey:
“Friend, what do you remember from the past?
“When I was a young deer, friend, sitting on the ground, I used to eat the topmost sprouts of this banyan tree.
That, friend, is what I remember from the past.”
Then, monks, the monkey and the elephant king asked the partridge:
“Friend, what do you remember from the past?
“In such-and-such a place, friends, there was a great banyan tree.”
"Then, having eaten the fruit, I voided my excrement in this spot;
from that, this banyan tree grew.
Therefore, O Noble One, I am greater by birth."
Then, monks, the monkey and the elephant king said this to the partridge:
“Friend, you are greater than us by birth.
We shall honor you, revere you, esteem you, and worship you; and we shall abide by your instruction.”
Then, monks, the partridge exhorted both the monkey and the elephant-nāga in the five precepts, and he himself lived having undertaken the five precepts.
Having lived with mutual respect, deference, and harmonious conduct toward one another, at the breaking up of the body after death, they were reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
Thus, monks, that was the holy life known as the "Partridge Way."
“Those people who are skilled in the Dhamma honor the aged;
they are praised in this very life.”
"And in the future life, a good destination.
For even those animals, monks, dwell with mutual respect, deference, and a sense of common purpose toward one another.

How then, monks, would it not be fitting for you—having gone forth in this well-expounded Dhamma and Vinaya—to dwell with mutual disrespect, lack of deference, and a lack of common purpose toward one another?
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
Having rebuked him...
and having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the monks:”
“I allow you, monks, salutation, rising up, joining of palms, respectful conduct, the best seat, the best water, and the best almsfood according to seniority.
But, monks, what belongs to the Saṅgha must not be withheld according to seniority.
Whoever should withhold it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.”
4. Persons Not to Be Saluted:
“Monks, these ten persons are not to be saluted:

one who was ordained later than another is not to be saluted by one who was ordained earlier; one who is not fully ordained is not to be saluted; one belonging to a different community is not to be saluted.”
One who speaks contrary to the Dhamma, even if senior, is not to be saluted; a woman is not to be saluted; a paṇḍaka is not to be saluted; one on probation is not to be saluted;
one deserving to be sent back to the beginning is not to be saluted; one deserving the trial period (mānatta) is not to be saluted; one undergoing the trial period is not to be saluted;
and one deserving rehabilitation is not to be saluted.
These, monks, are the ten who are not to be saluted.
There are, monks, these three who are to be saluted:
one ordained earlier is to be saluted by one ordained later; one belonging to a different community who is senior and speaks according to the Dhamma is to be saluted.
“Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is worthy of veneration in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins,
its devas and humans. These, bhikkhus, are the three who are worthy of veneration.”
5. The Refusal of Obstructing Seating.
Now at that time, people were preparing pavilions for the Saṅgha, preparing mats, and preparing open spaces.
The monks who were pupils of the group-of-six monks—
Thinking, “The Blessed One has authorized only what belongs to the Saṅgha to be used according to seniority,
not what is dedicated to a specific individual,” they went ahead of the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, taking possession of the pavilion, taking possession of the mats,
and taking possession of the space.
“This shall be for our preceptors; this shall be for our teachers; this shall be for us.

Then the Venerable Sāriputta, following closely behind the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, found no place when the decorated areas were already taken, the mats spread out were already taken, and the spots were already taken.
He sat down at the foot of a certain tree. Then,
as the night was drawing toward dawn, the Blessed One cleared his throat,
and the Venerable Sāriputta also cleared his throat.
“Who is here?
“It is I, Blessed One, Sāriputta.
“Why are you sitting here, Sāriputta?”
Then the Venerable Sāriputta reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, on this occasion and in this context, having had the community of monks assembled, questioned the monks:
"Is it true, monks, that the monks who are pupils of the group-of-six monks [acted in such a way]?"
"Does the Blessed One not allow that which belongs to the Saṅgha to be used according to seniority, rather than being designated for specific individuals?
Thus they went before the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha and took possession of the pavilion, took possession of the mats, and took possession of the space, saying:
"This shall be for our preceptors; this shall be for our teachers; this shall be for us."
“It is true, Blessed One,” [they replied].
Having rebuked them … and having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks, even that which has been set aside specifically for someone must not be withheld according to seniority.
Whoever should withhold it commits an offense of wrong-doing.
6. The Permission to Use Householder Cloth.
Now at that time, people were preparing high and luxurious seats in the dining hall within the village,

namely: a throne (āsandi), a divan (pallaṅka), a woolen rug (gonaka), a variegated rug (cittaka), a white woolen rug (paṭika), a cotton-padded rug (paṭalika), a stuffed mattress (tūlika), a bolster (vikatika),

one with long fleece on both sides (uddalomi), one with long fleece on one side only (ekantalomi), a grass mat (kaṭṭissa), silk (koseyya), embroidered cloth (kuttaka), an elephant rug (hatthatthara), a horse rug (assatthara), and a chariot rug (rathatthara).
There was a couch with a coverlet of antelope hide, spread with a choice rug of kadali-deer skin, provided with a canopy, and furnished with red pillows at both ends.
The monks, being scrupulous, did not sit down upon it.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, to sit upon a layperson’s luxury item, excluding three:
a high couch, a long chair, and a mattress stuffed with cotton wool;
but one must not lie down upon it.”
Now at that time, people were arranging cotton-padded couches and chairs in the dining hall within the village.
The bhikkhus, being afraid of wrongdoing, did not sit down.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, to sit on what has been prepared by a householder, but not to lie down upon it.
Then the Blessed One, wandering by stages on his tour, arrived at Sāvatthī. He stayed at the Jeta Grove Monastery. Thereupon, the Blessed One expressed his appreciation for the Jeta Grove Monastery.
There the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept my meal tomorrow together with the community of bhikkhus.
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, understanding the Blessed One’s consent, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to his right, and departed.
Then, at the end of that night, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika had various kinds of fine food, both hard and soft, prepared and had the time announced to the Blessed One:
"It is time, venerable sir; the meal is ready.

Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to the residence of the householder Anāthapiṇḍika. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat together with the community of monks.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, having personally served and satisfied the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha with excellent hard and soft foods,
sat down to one side when the Blessed One had finished his meal and had put away his bowl and hand.
As he was sitting there, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika said this to the Blessed One:
“How, venerable sir, should I proceed regarding Jetavana?
“In that case, householder, establish Jetavana for the Saṅgha of the four quarters, both those who have come and those yet to come.
“Yes, venerable sir,” Anāthapiṇḍika the householder replied to the Blessed One, and he established Jetavana for the Saṅgha of the four quarters, both those who had come and those yet to come.
Then the Blessed One expressed his appreciation to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika with these verses:
"It wards off cold and heat,
and likewise wild beasts;"
From snakes and mosquitoes,
from cold and also rains;
then there is the terrible wind and sun.
What has arisen is struck down—
for the sake of a shelter, for the sake of happiness,
and in order to meditate and to attain insight.
The gift of a monastery to the Saṅgha was praised as the foremost by the Buddha;
therefore, a wise person...
Perceiving his own welfare,
one should have delightful monasteries built and cause those who are learned to dwell therein.
To those who have become upright, one should give food and drink, as well as clothing and lodgings.
With a serene mind,
they teach him the Dhamma that removes all suffering.
“Having understood that Dhamma here,
he attains final Nibbāna, free from taints.
Then the Blessed One, having expressed his appreciation to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika with these verses, rose from his seat and departed.
8. Obstructing Seating, etc.
Now at that time, a certain high official who was a lay follower of the Ājīvakas had a meal prepared for the Saṅgha.
The Venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta arrived late and, finding the meal already underway, made the monk sitting next to him leave his seat.
A great clamor arose in the assembly of the reciters.
Then that chief minister complained, grumbled, and expressed his indignation:
“How can these ascetics, followers of the Sakyan son, come later and cause the monk sitting immediately next to them to rise when the meal is unfinished?”
“There was a great commotion in the hall of the meal-offering.
Is it not possible to eat as much as one desires while sitting elsewhere?
The monks heard that high official complaining, grumbling, and expressing his indignation.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires... [and so on]... complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son, having arrived later, cause a bhikkhu who was sitting immediately next to him to rise from a meal that had not yet been concluded?
There was a great clamor in the dining hall!"
Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Is it true, Upananda, that you, having arrived late, made the monk sitting next to you rise from his meal while the food was still unfinished, so that there was a commotion in the dining hall?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“… How can you, foolish man, having arrived late, cause a bhikkhu who was sitting immediately next to you to rise when his meal is unfinished?
The dining hall has been thrown into a state of clamor.”
"This, foolish man, will not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
Having rebuked him...
and having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks, a monk who has not finished his meal should not be asked to give the full admission (*upasaṃpadā*).
Whoever should ask him, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If he does ask him, and [the candidate] has already been invited to eat, he should be told: ‘Go, fetch some water.’”
If one obtains it in this way, that is good.
If one does not obtain it, one should swallow the rice thoroughly and give the seat to the elder bhikkhu.
Monks, I say that by no means whatsoever should the seat of an elder bhikkhu be withheld.
‘Whoever should prevent [him from leaving], there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks were causing sick monks to rise.
The sick ones spoke thus:
“We are not able to get up, friend; we are ill.
[The others] say, “We will help the venerable ones to get up,” and having taken hold of them and helped them to stand, they let go while they are still standing.
The sick ones faint and fall down.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, one who is sick should not be ordained.
Whoever should ordain him, there is an offense of wrong-doing.”
Now at that time, the group of six monks,
thinking, "We are ill and should not be disturbed," obstructed superior beds.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, to give a suitable bed to one who is ill.
Now at that time, the group of six monks reserved lodgings by means of a pretext.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, a dwelling should not be reserved by means of a pretext.
Whoever should so reserve it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, the group of seventeen monks were repairing a certain remote large monastery.
“Here we shall spend the rains retreat.
The group of six monks saw the group of seventeen monks repairing the dwelling,
and having seen them, they said this:
“Friends, these seventeen monks from the group of seventeen are repairing the monastery.
Come, let us rouse them.
Some spoke thus:
“Wait, friends, until they have repaired it; once it has been repaired, we will ask them to leave.
Then the group-of-six monks said this to the group-of-seventeen monks:
“Get up, friends, our dwelling is now reached.”
“Friend, should this not have been pointed out beforehand?
We would have prepared something else.
“Friend, is this not a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha?”
“It belongs to the Saṅgha, friend.
“Get up, friend, our monastery has come into our possession.
“The monastery is large, friend.”
"You may stay here too; we shall stay as well.
"Get up, friends! This monastery belongs to us! they say, and being angry and displeased, they grab them by the neck and drag them out.
As they are being dragged out, they weep.
The bhikkhus said, “Friends,
why are you weeping? “Friends,
these bhikkhus of the group of six, angry and displeased, are throwing us out from our dwellings belonging to the Saṅgha.”
Those monks who were of few desires... [as before] ... complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can the group-of-six monks, being angry and displeased, actually eject monks from dwellings belonging to the Saṅgha?
Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One... [as before].
“Is it true, monks, that you, being angry and displeased, have actually driven monks out from a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha?
“It is true, Blessed One.
… [after rebuking them] … pe …
Having given a Dhamma talk, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is angry and displeased must not eject another bhikkhu from a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha.
Whoever should eject him is to be dealt with according to the rule.”
“I allow you, monks, to take possession of lodgings. Then, this thought occurred to the monks: [“Who shall assign the lodgings? 9.
The Appointment of a Lodging Assigner.
Then, this thought occurred to the monks: [“Who shall assign the lodgings?”]
“By whom, then, should the lodgings be assigned?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One... [and the Blessed One said:
“Monks, I allow you to appoint a monk endowed with five qualities as the assigner of lodgings:”

One who would not go astray through favoritism, nor go astray through hatred, nor go astray through delusion, nor go astray through fear, and who knows what has been accepted and what has not been accepted—such a person, monks, should be appointed in this way:
First, a monk should be requested; having been requested, a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
‘Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha appoint the monk named so-and-so as the assigner of lodgings.
This is the motion.
"Let the Sangha hear me, venerable sirs.
The Sangha appoints the bhikkhu named so-and-so as the assigner of lodgings.
Whosoever among the venerable ones approves of the appointment of the bhikkhu named so-and-so as the assigner of lodgings, let him be silent."
"Whoever does not approve, let him speak.
The Saṅgha has appointed the bhikkhu named so-and-so as the assigner of lodgings.
It is approved by the Saṅgha; therefore, by silence, I hold it to be so."
Then it occurred to the monks who were assigners of lodgings,
"How, indeed, should the lodgings be assigned?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, first to count the monks; having counted the monks, to count the lodgings; having counted the lodgings, to assign them by way of the lodgings.
While they were assigning them by way of the lodgings, they exceeded the number of lodgings...
[omission] ... “I allow you, monks, to assign them by way of the dwellings.”
When they were assigning [the dwellings] by vihāra, the vihāras were left empty...
[as before] ... "I allow you, monks, to assign them by pariveṇa.
When they were assigning them by pariveṇa, the pariveṇas were left empty... [as before] ...
“I allow you, monks, to give even a portion.
When a portion has been taken and another monk arrives, it must not be given against his will.
Now at that time, monks were taking lodgings for one who was standing outside the boundary.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one should not assign a lodging to someone standing outside the boundary.
Whoever should so assign it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.”
Now at that time, the monks, having taken possession of lodgings, reserved them for all times.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, having taken possession of a lodging, it should not be reserved for all times.”
"Whoever should prevent [the robe] would commit an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
I allow you, monks, to prevent it for the three months of the rains, but not during the time of the seasons.
Then, this thought occurred to the monks:
“How many, then, are the ways of taking up lodgings?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, there are three ways of taking up lodgings:”
There is the first, the last, and the one released in between.
When the Āsāḷhī full moon has passed by one day, the first [robe] should be taken up.
When the Āsāḷhī full moon has arrived at the month [of its occurrence], the last [robe] should be taken up.
When the invitation ceremony has passed, a temporary assignment for the dwelling should be taken for the purpose of the future rains residence.
These, monks, are the three ways of assigning dwellings.
The second recitation section is finished.
Now at that time, the Venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta, having taken a lodging in Sāvatthī, went to a certain village residence.
There too he took a lodging.
Then it occurred to those monks:
“Friends, this venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta is a maker of quarrels, a maker of strife, a maker of disputes, a maker of contention, and a creator of legal issues in the Saṅgha.
If he stays here for the rains retreat, none of us will be at ease.
Come, let us ask him.”
Then those bhikkhus said this to the venerable Upananda the Sakyan:
"Friend Upananda, did you not take a lodging in Sāvatthī?
"It is so, friends," he replied.
“But why, friend Upananda, do you exclude two when you are alone?
“In this case, friend, I let go;
in that case, I take hold,” he replied.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires … [as before] … were indignant, disparaged, and complained, saying:
“How can the venerable Upananda the Sakyan-son refuse two [people] while alone?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One … [as before] …
“Is it true, Upananda, that you alone prevent two [monks] from entering?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him... [as before]...
How can it be, you foolish man, that you alone shall exclude two people?
In this matter, what was taken by you there has been relinquished here; what was taken by you here has been relinquished there.
Thus, you foolish man, you are excluded from both places.
“This is not for the inspiration of those without faith, foolish man,” he said.
Having rebuked him and given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks, one person must not be prevented from entering by another.
Whoever should prevent him, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, the Blessed One was giving a discourse on the Vinaya to the monks in many ways, concerning the Vinaya.
He speaks in praise of the Vinaya; he speaks in praise of the mastery of the Vinaya; again and again he speaks in praise of the Venerable Upāli. The monks thought:

"The Blessed One has indeed spoken on the subject of the Vinaya in many ways; he speaks in praise of the Vinaya; he speaks in praise of the mastery of the Vinaya; again and again he speaks in praise of the Venerable Upāli."
"Come, friends, let us master the Vinaya in the presence of the Venerable Upāli.
So many bhikkhus—elders, juniors, and those of middle standing—mastered the Vinaya in the presence of the Venerable Upāli.
Out of respect for the elder bhikkhus, the Venerable Upāli recited the text while remaining standing.
The elder monks, out of respect for the Dhamma, continued to recite the rules while standing.
Consequently, both the elder monks and the Venerable Upāli became exhausted.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow, monks, a junior monk who is reciting to sit on an equal seat, or on a higher seat out of reverence for the Dhamma;
and an elder monk who is having [the text] recited to him to sit on an equal seat, or on a lower seat out of reverence for the Dhamma.
Now at that time, many monks standing near the Venerable Upāli grew weary while waiting for the recitation.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to sit together with those who share a common seat,” he said.
Then it occurred to the monks:
“To what extent, indeed, is one considered a ‘sharer of the same seat’?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, I allow you to sit together with one who is within three years of seniority.”
Now at that time, several monks who shared a common seat sat upon a couch and broke the couch; they sat upon a bench and broke the bench.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a couch for a group of three, and a bench for a group of three.”
Even when three groups sat on a bed, they broke the bed; when they sat on a bench, they broke the bench...
[and so forth] ... "I allow you, monks, a bed for two groups and a bench for two groups.
Now at that time, the monks were apprehensive about sitting together with those who did not share a common seat on a long seat.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, to sit on a long seat together with those who do not share a common seat, except for a paṇḍaka, a woman, and a hermaphrodite.
Then it occurred to the monks:
“How long, then, is the minimum length for a long seat?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow that which is sufficient for three people; this is the minimum length for a long seat.”
Now at that time, Visākhā Migāramātā desired to have a gabled mansion with elephant-trunk turrets built for the sake of the Saṅgha.
Then it occurred to the bhikkhus:
"Has the use of a mansion been permitted by the Blessed One, or has it not been permitted?"
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow the use of all palaces,” he said.
Now at that time, King Pasenadi of Kosala’s grandmother had passed away.
Upon his death, a great quantity of unallowable goods came into the possession of the Saṅgha,
namely: high couches, luxurious couches, woolen rugs, embroidered rugs, cotton rugs, rugs with long hair, rugs with hair on one side,
rugs with hair on both sides, rugs made of animal fur, silk garments, brocades, elephant blankets, horse blankets, and chariot rugs.
It had a covering of antelope hide, a choice spread of kadali-deer skin, with a canopy above and red cushions at both ends.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.

“Monks, I allow you to use a high chair after cutting off its legs, to use a couch after tearing out its hair-wool stuffing, to make a bolster by unstuffing a mattress, and to use the remainder as a floor-cover.”
1. On that occasion, at a certain village residence not far from Sāvatthī, the resident monks were distressed while assigning lodgings to visiting and departing monks.
Then it occurred to those monks:
“Friends, we are currently overwhelmed by having to prepare lodgings for visiting and departing monks.
Come now, friends, let us give all the lodgings belonging to the Saṅgha to one person;
we shall then enjoy what belongs to him.”
They gave all that monastic lodging belonging to the Saṅgha to a single person.
When visiting monks approached those monks, they said to them,
"Friends, please prepare a lodging for us."
“There is no lodging belonging to the Saṅgha, friend;
everything has been given by us to a single person.
“But, friends, would you give away a lodging belonging to the Saṅgha?”
“Yes, friends,” they replied.
Then those monks who were few in desires... [as before]... complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“How can these monks dispose of a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha?”
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One … [as before] … “Is it true,
bhikkhus, that bhikkhus are disposing of lodgings belonging to the Saṅgha?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“...How, monks, can those foolish men dispose of a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha?
This, monks, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence... [and so on].
Having rebuked them … and having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, there are these five things that are not to be relinquished; they must not be relinquished by a Saṅgha, a group, or an individual.”
Even those things that have been relinquished are as if not relinquished.
Whoever should relinquish them commits a *thullaccaya* offense.
Which five?
A monastery and the site of a monastery—this is the first thing that is not to be disposed of; it must not be disposed of by a Saṅgha, a group, or an individual.
Even if it has been disposed of, it remains undispensed.
Whoever should dispose of it commits a thullaccaya offense.
A monastery or the site of a monastery—this is the second thing not to be disposed of; it must not be disposed of by a Saṅgha, a group, or an individual.
Even if it has been relinquished, it is as if not relinquished.
Whoever should relinquish it incurs a thullaccaya offense.
[This applies to] a bed, a chair, a mattress, or a pillow.
This is the third thing that must not be relinquished; it is not to be relinquished by a Saṅgha, a group, or an individual.
Even if it has been relinquished, it remains unrelinquished.
Whoever should relinquish it commits a thullaccaya offense.
The iron cauldron, the iron pot, the iron bowl, the iron pan, the adze, the axe, the hatchet, the spade, and the chisel—this is the fourth item that is not to be disposed of;
it must not be disposed of by a Saṅgha, a group, or an individual.
Even if it has been disposed of, it remains undispensed.
Whoever should dispose of it commits a *thullaccaya* offense.
A creeper, bamboo, *muñja* grass, *pabbaja* grass, grass, clay, wooden articles, and earthenware articles—this is the fifth class of things that must not be disposed of;
they are not to be disposed of by a Saṅgha, a group, or an individual.
Even when given away, it remains as if not given away.
Whoever should give it away commits a grave offense (thullaccaya).
These, monks, are the five things that are not to be given away; they must not be given away by a Saṅgha, a group, or an individual.
“Even those things that have been distributed are as if not distributed.
Whoever should distribute them, there is an offense of thullaccaya.
2. The Matter of Non-Sharing.

Sāriputta and Moggallāna have evil desires; they have fallen under the sway of evil desires.

3. The Discourse on the Assignment of Building Work.
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Kīṭāgiri for as long as he pleased, set out on a wandering tour toward Āḷavī.
Wandering by stages, he eventually arrived at Āḷavī.
At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava Shrine.
Now on that occasion, the monks of Āḷavī were assigning such works as these:
they would assign work even for the mere act of setting down alms-food.
They grant *navakamma* even for the mere act of plastering with mortar;
they grant *navakamma* even for the mere act of installing a door;
they grant *navakamma* even for the mere act of making a door-bolt groove.
They grant new work merely for the purpose of making a window-opening;
they grant new work merely for the purpose of making it white-colored;
they grant new work merely for the purpose of making it black-colored.
They grant new work even for merely applying red chalk as a preparation;
they grant new work even for merely roofing;
they grant new work even for merely binding.
They grant *navakamma* even for the mere act of placing a store of materials;
they grant *navakamma* even for the mere act of repairing broken or dilapidated parts;
they grant *navakamma* even for the mere act of making a border or molding.
They give twenty-year tasks;
they give thirty-year tasks;
they even give lifelong tasks.
They were giving new construction work for a monastery that was finished only as far as the stage of smoke.
Those monks who were of few desires... [as before] ...they complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
"How can the monks of Āḷavī give such new construction work as this?"
They will show their appreciation for new work even by the mere act of throwing down a lump of clay;
even by the mere act of plastering a wall;
even by the mere act of setting up a door.
Even by merely making a door-bolt recess,
even by merely making a window-opening,
even by merely applying a white coating...
Even by merely making it black in color...
even by merely applying red ochre...
even by merely covering it...
Even by merely binding [the roof],
even by merely setting down bundles [of materials],
even by merely repairing what is broken or dilapidated...
Even by merely making a border [around the robe],
even for one who has been ordained for twenty years,
even for one who has been ordained for thirty years...

“They will show the new construction work on a monastery that has been finished for as long as a lifetime, or even for a mere period of smoke. They reported this matter to the Blessed One … [as before] … The Blessed One said: “Monks, a monastery that has been finished for as long as a lifetime, or even for a mere period of smoke, should not be shown. Whoever should show it: an offense of wrong-doing. Then a certain monk had a monastery built; having had it built, he did not show it. The people asked him: “Venerable sir, why do you not show the monastery? He replied: “Friends, the Blessed One has prohibited showing a monastery that has been finished for as long as a lifetime, or even for a mere period of smoke. The people said: “Venerable sir, when was this monastery finished? Was it finished yesterday, or the day before yesterday, or the day before that? He replied: “Friends, it was finished so-and-so many years ago. The people said: “Venerable sir, this monastery was finished so long ago, yet you do not show it! Come, let us destroy it!
